opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to frame it is: the real world is the bottleneck. Every interaction with it costs something, whether that's time, money, wear on a robot, or, in the case of anything involving people, real consequences if you get it wrong. So the question becomes how you do as much of the learning as possible *before* you ever touch reality, and then make the little real experience you do get count for as much as it can.

To me that splits into a few pieces. The first is simulation and, more broadly, learned or procedurally generated environments. If you can build a distribution of environments rich enough that the real world looks like just another sample from it, then an agent trained across that distribution should transfer. That's the idea behind things like domain randomization and unsupervised environment design: rather than hand-crafting one simulator and hoping it's accurate, you let an adversary or a curriculum generator propose environments right at the edge of what the agent can handle. You're not trying to be perfectly realistic, you're trying to be *robustly* general.

The second piece is meta-learning, or learning to learn. If the real-world budget is tiny, you want an agent whose prior already encodes how to adapt quickly. So you push the expensive part, the outer loop, into simulation, and what you get out is something like a learned learning algorithm that's sample-efficient at deployment time. Some of our work on learned optimizers and discovered RL objectives comes from exactly that motivation. Can we discover better algorithms in cheap settings that then generalize to the expensive ones?

The third piece, which I think people underrate, is the multi-agent side. A lot of the costly experience in the real world involves other agents, other people. You can't just collect millions of episodes of interacting with humans. So you need things like zero-shot coordination, policies that can work with partners they've never met, because you won't get to fine-tune on each new human. Self-play by itself tends to produce brittle, arbitrary conventions. That's fine in a two-player zero-sum game, but it's a disaster when you need to coordinate with someone outside your training loop.

And underneath all of it is scale on the compute side. Hardware-accelerated environments, running everything end-to-end on GPUs in JAX, mean a simulated sample is now incredibly cheap. That changes the economics. If simulated experience is effectively free and real experience is precious, the research agenda becomes: what do you have to get right in the cheap world so the expensive world is mostly a confirmation and not a training ground?

So in short, I frame it as an asymmetry problem. Make the cheap experience as diverse and adversarial as possible, learn priors and algorithms rather than just policies, and treat the real world as the test set you only get to look at sparingly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the cost of gathering real-world experience and the value of simulation, but does not observe that machine learning’s success with real-world data has been in settings where the data was already supplied.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that the fundamental resource in reinforcement learning is interaction, and in the real world interaction is slow, costly, sometimes dangerous, and you can't rewind. Robots break, clinical trials take years, you can't run a million episodes of a financial market. So the question becomes: where do you get the experience you need to learn, if not from the world directly?

And I think there are really two complementary answers. The first is simulation. If you can build a simulator that captures the structure of the problem, you can generate experience at an enormous rate, and with modern hardware, if you write the environment itself to run on the accelerator, you can get thousands of times more throughput than the classic setup where the environment lives on a CPU and the policy on a GPU. That changes what kinds of research questions you can even ask. Things like meta-learning or learning the learning algorithm itself, which need orders of magnitude more samples than just training one policy, suddenly become tractable.

But the second answer, and the one I find more interesting scientifically, is that you have to ask what the experience is actually for. Often the cheap experience you can generate, in simulation or from historical logs, doesn't match the situation you'll be deployed in. So the challenge isn't just "get more data," it's "learn something that transfers." That's where you get into questions of generalisation, of designing distributions of training problems rather than single problems, so that the agent learns robust strategies instead of exploiting the quirks of one environment. If you only train on one setting, the agent will overfit to it, and worse, it will find the bugs in your simulator and exploit those.

And then, especially in multi-agent settings, there's a third layer, which is that part of the environment is other agents, humans included, and you can't simulate them perfectly either. So you need methods that don't assume you've seen your partner before, that are robust to the fact that the real world will contain policies you never trained against. A lot of my work on zero-shot coordination comes from exactly that framing.

So, to sum up, I'd say the challenge is really about turning a sample-efficiency problem into a problem-design problem. Rather than squeezing a little more out of each expensive real interaction, you ask: what cheap experience could I generate such that the thing I learn still holds when it meets reality? And I think the honest answer is that we're still quite far from having principled tools for that, which is what makes it an exciting place to work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses costly real-world interaction and mentions historical logs as a source of cheap experience, but it does not say that machine learning has succeeded with real-world data when that data was already supplied.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: how much can you learn from each interaction with the world? In reinforcement learning, we often focus on whether an algorithm eventually solves a task, but if that takes an enormous amount of experience, it may not be a useful solution in practice.

So you have to think about what knowledge you can bring to the problem, how you reuse the data you already have, and which new interactions are actually worth collecting. Exploration becomes a question of gathering information that will improve your decisions, while accounting for the cost of getting that information. There's a trade-off there: doing more computation can be worthwhile if it saves you an expensive real-world experiment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reusing existing data and the cost of collecting new interactions, but does not observe that machine learning’s success with real-world data has occurred in settings where the data was already supplied.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much useful learning you can extract from each interaction. In reinforcement learning, we often think about an agent trying things repeatedly, but in the real world those attempts can take time, cost money, or have consequences. So you have to care about which experiences you collect, how you reuse them, and what prior knowledge you bring to the problem.

One way to frame it is as learning how to learn: can experience across related tasks give you a learning procedure that adapts quickly to a new situation? That doesn’t remove the need for exploration, but it changes the starting point. You’re trying to make those first few interactions informative, rather than having to discover everything from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response discusses costly real-world interactions and how to select or reuse experience, but does not state that machine learning has succeeded with real-world data when that data is already supplied.
